findings.title: Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) via Disabled Template Escaping
findings.discovered_by: App-wide configuration reviewer: app-wide setup
findings.description: The template engine is configured with auto-escaping disabled in server.js:137, which allows for reflected or stored XSS attacks if any user-provided content is rendered in views.
steps_to_exploit: Find an input field that is rendered back to the user via Swig templates.
Submit a script payload (e.g., <script>alert(1)</script>).
View the page where the input is rendered; the payload executes in the victim's browser.
findings.impact: Full account takeover, session theft, and unauthorized actions on behalf of the user.

findings.title: Session fixation vulnerability due to failure to regenerate session ID
findings.discovered_by: Access control reviewer: POST /login; Credentials, sessions and the login flow reviewer: POST /login
findings.description: The login handler at app/routes/session.js:53-119 assigns a userId to the existing session without regenerating it upon successful authentication. This allows an attacker who has pre-captured a session cookie (or forced one onto a victim) to retain that same session identifier after the victim logs in, effectively hijacking the authenticated session.
steps_to_exploit: Attacker visits the site to obtain a session cookie.
Attacker forces this known session ID onto the victim's browser.
Victim logs in to the application.
Attacker uses the same session ID to access the victim's authenticated account.
findings.impact: Account takeover and unauthorized access to user data.

findings.title: Information disclosure via distinct login error messages
findings.discovered_by: Access control reviewer: POST /login
findings.description: The login handler differentiates between 'Invalid username' and 'Invalid password' error messages in app/routes/session.js:82-98. By observing different responses, an attacker can confirm the existence of specific usernames in the database.
steps_to_exploit: Submit a login request with a known or guessed username and a dummy password.
Observe the error message received.
Submit a login request with a random/non-existent username.
If the error message changes, the attacker confirms the validity of the username in step 1.
findings.impact: Username enumeration, facilitating brute-force or targeted credential stuffing attacks.

findings.title: Unsafe NoSQL query construction
findings.discovered_by: Untrusted input reaching an interpreter reviewer: POST /login
findings.description: The 'userName' input from the request body is passed directly to the 'usersCol.findOne' MongoDB query at app/data/user-dao.js:91. If the database driver or configuration is susceptible to object injection (e.g., passing { $gt: '' } as the username), an attacker can bypass authentication without knowing a valid username.
steps_to_exploit: Send a POST request to /login
Set the 'userName' parameter to a JSON object: {"$gt": ""}
The application will find the first user in the database, potentially allowing login as the first user (often an administrator).
findings.impact: Authentication bypass, potentially leading to unauthorized access to administrator accounts.

findings.title: Unrestricted Registration of New Accounts
findings.discovered_by: Access control reviewer: POST /signup
findings.description: The POST /signup route has no protection (e.g., CSRF tokens or reCAPTCHA), allowing automated scripts or attackers to bulk-create user accounts. The app-wide CSRF middleware is commented out, and no specific rate-limiting exists for this route.
steps_to_exploit: Send a series of POST requests to /signup with generated username/password combinations.
Observe that the application successfully creates new user accounts without validation of human presence or anti-automation tokens.
findings.impact: Resource exhaustion and database bloat; potential for spamming or malicious account takeovers.

findings.title: Unsafe rendering of user input in template
findings.discovered_by: Untrusted input reaching an interpreter reviewer: POST /signup
findings.description: The application renders user-supplied input ('userName' and 'email' via 'errors' object) directly into the signup template in app/routes/session.js:214 and app/routes/session.js:249. Because XSS protections (helmet.xssFilter) are disabled in server.js, an attacker can inject malicious scripts into the signup form fields, which will be reflected back to the user or an administrator viewing the rendered page.
steps_to_exploit: Navigate to the signup page.
Submit a signup request with a crafted payload in the 'userName' field (e.g., <script>alert(document.cookie)</script>).
The server returns the template with the payload injected into the view, executing the script in the victim's browser.
findings.impact: Account takeover via session cookie theft or redirection to malicious sites.

findings.title: Catastrophic ReDoS via Unsafe Regular Expression
findings.discovered_by: Untrusted input reaching an interpreter reviewer: POST /profile
findings.description: The application performs a regular expression test on user-supplied 'bankRouting' input using a pattern containing nested quantifiers: /([0-9]+)+\#/. This is vulnerable to catastrophic backtracking, where crafted input (e.g., a long string of digits without a trailing '#') causes the event loop to block, resulting in a Denial of Service. This is defined in app/routes/profile.js:59.
steps_to_exploit: Navigate to the profile update page.
Submit a request with the 'bankRouting' parameter set to a long string of digits (e.g., '1' repeated 50 times) without a trailing '#' character.
Observe the application process become unresponsive as the CPU usage spikes to 100% due to regex backtracking.
findings.impact: An attacker can render the application service unavailable to all users by forcing high CPU consumption.

findings.title: Server-Side JavaScript Injection via eval()
findings.discovered_by: Untrusted input reaching an interpreter reviewer: POST /contributions
findings.description: The application uses `eval()` on unsanitized user-provided input from `req.body` in `app/routes/contributions.js` lines 32-34. This allows an attacker to execute arbitrary JavaScript code within the context of the Node.js process.
steps_to_exploit: Navigate to the contributions update endpoint.
Craft a malicious POST request where the parameters 'preTax', 'afterTax', or 'roth' contain executable JavaScript code (e.g., '1; require("child_process").execSync("ls")').
Observe that the input is passed directly to the `eval()` function, executing the payload.
findings.impact: Full system compromise. An attacker can execute arbitrary OS commands, access the filesystem, steal environment variables, or exfiltrate database contents.

evidence.quote: const preTax = eval(req.body.preTax); const afterTax = eval(req.body.afterTax); const roth = eval(req.body.roth);

findings.title: Insecure Direct Object Reference (IDOR) in allocations route
findings.discovered_by: Access control reviewer: GET /allocations/:userId
findings.description: The application trusts the `userId` provided in the request parameters to fetch data, rather than using the authenticated `userId` from the session. Even though the `isLoggedIn` middleware ensures the user is logged in, any authenticated user can view the allocations of any other user by simply changing the `userId` in the URL.
steps_to_exploit: Log in to the application as a standard user.
Navigate to /allocations/<your_user_id> to observe your own data.
Change the URL to /allocations/<target_user_id> to access another user's allocation records.
findings.impact: Unauthorized access to sensitive personal allocation and user data (names, IDs, financial-related data) of any other user in the system.

findings.title: NoSQL Injection via $where operator
findings.discovered_by: Untrusted input reaching an interpreter reviewer: GET /allocations/:userId
findings.description: The application uses string concatenation to build a MongoDB $where query clause using user-supplied input 'threshold' in app/data/allocations-dao.js:78. Because the input is not sanitized or validated, an attacker can break out of the string literal and inject arbitrary JavaScript code that will be executed by the database engine.
steps_to_exploit: Access the /allocations/:userId endpoint.
Provide a 'threshold' query parameter crafted with a JavaScript payload, for example: ?threshold=1'; return true; //
Observe the database returning all records regardless of user ownership or threshold criteria due to the injected 'return true'.
findings.impact: An attacker can bypass data filtering, potentially accessing all allocations in the database or performing unauthorized data exfiltration.

findings.title: Broken Access Control: Exposure of all memos to all authenticated users
findings.discovered_by: Access control reviewer: GET /memos
findings.description: The `displayMemos` handler fetches all memos from the database using `memosDAO.getAllMemos` without filtering by the `userId` stored in the session. Although the route is protected by `isLoggedIn`, any authenticated user can view all memos created by all other users in the system.
steps_to_exploit: Log into the application with a valid user account.
Navigate to the /memos route.
Observe that memos belonging to other users are visible in the response.
findings.impact: Unauthorized disclosure of sensitive information contained in memos belonging to other users.

findings.title: Broken Access Control - Insecure Object Association
findings.discovered_by: Access control reviewer: POST /memos
findings.description: The `addMemos` handler at `app/routes/memos.js:13` accepts user-supplied data and inserts it into the database without associating the record with the authenticated user from the session. While the `isLoggedIn` middleware ensures the user is authenticated, the DAO does not enforce ownership. This allows any authenticated user to potentially influence or pollute the shared `memos` collection without logical separation, as the `memosDAO.insert` method only stores the memo body and a timestamp.
steps_to_exploit: Authenticate as a standard user via a valid login session.
Submit a POST request to /memos with an arbitrary memo body.
Observe that the application accepts and stores the data without linking it to the specific user ID available in the session.
findings.impact: Data integrity compromise and potential information leakage if the application assumes memos are private while the underlying storage is global/unscoped.

findings.title: Insecure Session Configuration: resave and saveUninitialized enabled
findings.discovered_by: Credentials, sessions and the login flow reviewer: GET /; Credentials, sessions and the login flow reviewer: GET /dashboard
findings.description: The session middleware is configured with 'resave: true' and 'saveUninitialized: true' in server.js:78. This can lead to race conditions, unnecessary session store load, and the creation of empty session entries for unauthenticated users, which may facilitate session fixation or resource exhaustion.
steps_to_exploit: Attacker repeatedly visits the application to generate large numbers of empty session entries in the server-side store.
The application keeps these sessions active due to saveUninitialized: true, potentially leading to denial of service on the session store.
findings.impact: Increased risk of session fixation and resource exhaustion on the session storage backend.

findings.title: Sensitive Data Stored in Plaintext
findings.discovered_by: Credentials, sessions and the login flow reviewer: POST /profile
findings.description: The application fails to encrypt sensitive personal information including SSN and Date of Birth before storing them in the database. The security measures intended to encrypt this data are explicitly commented out at app/data/profile-dao.js:67-76.
steps_to_exploit: Log in as an authenticated user.
Submit a POST request to /profile containing sensitive PII in the 'ssn' or 'dob' fields.
Access the underlying database to observe the sensitive data stored in plaintext.
findings.impact: In the event of a database compromise, attacker access to PII leads to severe identity theft risks for users.

rejected.title: Missing Security Headers
rejected.claim: Essential security headers provided by the helmet middleware are all commented out in server.js. This exposes the application to various attacks such as XSS, clickjacking, and MIME-sniffing.
rejected.why: the reviewer's quotes do not exist in the files named
rejected.reasoning: The application's `server.js` explicitly comments out the initialization of `helmet` and its associated security middleware (CSP, frameguard, etc.). As a result, the application lacks essential security headers, confirming the claim that protections against XSS, clickjacking, and MIME-sniffing are currently disabled.

rejected.title: Session Cookies Missing 'Secure' and 'HttpOnly' Flags
rejected.claim: The session management middleware is initialized without securing cookies. The 'secure' and 'httpOnly' flags are absent in the default configuration, making cookies accessible via JavaScript and transmittable over unencrypted HTTP.
rejected.why: the reviewer's quotes do not exist in the files named
rejected.reasoning: The application uses the 'express-session' middleware without configuring the 'cookie' object to include 'httpOnly: true' or 'secure: true'. These security flags are commented out in server.js, leaving the session cookie vulnerable to access via client-side JavaScript and transmission over insecure HTTP connections.

rejected.title: CSRF protection disabled app-wide
rejected.claim: The CSRF protection middleware is explicitly commented out in server.js:107, rendering the application vulnerable to Cross-Site Request Forgery for any state-changing operations that might exist or be added, and potentially impacting the integrity of session-based actions.
rejected.why: the reviewer's quotes are comments, not live code
rejected.reasoning: The CSRF protection middleware is explicitly commented out in server.js, and no other state-changing routes implement manual anti-CSRF token verification. The application processes POST requests based only on session cookies, making it vulnerable to CSRF.

rejected.title: Unvalidated Redirect Based on User Data
rejected.claim: The application redirects users to either '/benefits' or '/dashboard' based on the 'isAdmin' property of the user object retrieved from the database. Because the 'isAdmin' property is retrieved directly from the database and used to control the flow of the application without further validation or consideration for untrusted database content, it creates an open redirect path if the database is compromised or if 'isAdmin' is erroneously set.
rejected.why: the code contradicts the claim or already contains the protection
rejected.reasoning: The application redirects users to fixed internal routes ('/benefits' or '/dashboard') at line 117. There is no user-controlled URL input involved in the redirect logic, and the redirect target is determined solely by hardcoded paths, making an open redirect attack impossible.

rejected.title: Missing CSRF Protection
rejected.claim: The CSRF protection middleware is explicitly commented out in server.js:107, leaving the application vulnerable to cross-site request forgery. While this route is a GET, the lack of global CSRF protection affects the entire application security posture.
rejected.why: the reviewer's quotes do not exist in the files named
rejected.reasoning: The application lacks CSRF protection as the `csurf` middleware is explicitly commented out in `server.js` (lines 107-113). Since no other CSRF protection is implemented or enforced, state-changing POST requests (e.g., contribution updates in `contributions.js`) are vulnerable to cross-site request forgery when an authenticated user visits a malicious page.

While the route might be intended for public content, the lack of any authorization middleware means that if any tutorial pages contain sensitive information or should only be accessible to logged-in users, there is no enforcement mechanism to restrict access.

The routes are intended for public educational access, as stated in the project README, and do not handle sensitive user data that requires authentication.

rejected.claim: The CSRF protection middleware is explicitly commented out in server.js:107. As a result, the session-based state changing or sensitive actions performed via the dashboard are vulnerable to CSRF attacks.

rejected.title: Lack of Session Security Configuration (Security Headers)
rejected.claim: Essential security headers including HSTS and no-cache are disabled or commented out in server.js (e.g., lines 48, 54). This increases the risk of session hijacking via man-in-the-middle attacks or cached sensitive profile data remaining on shared machines.
rejected.why: the reviewer's quotes are comments, not live code
rejected.reasoning: The application lacks security headers, including HSTS and cache control, as the `helmet` middleware setup in `server.js` (lines 45-64) is explicitly commented out. Consequently, these headers are never sent to the client, confirming the vulnerability as described.

rejected.title: Insecure Session Persistence After Logout
rejected.claim: The application-wide session middleware is configured with 'resave: true', which can lead to session fixation or continuation issues if the application does not explicitly destroy the session object upon logout. Without explicit code to regenerate the session ID upon login or destroy it fully on logout, session state may persist unexpectedly.
